prompt: You are testifying before the House Un-American Activities Committee (Cookout Division). It has been alleged that you have referred to the Fourth of July as 'the holidays.' Respond to the committee.
response:
*adjusts microphone, glances at counsel*

Mr. Chairman, members of the committee—

I am here under oath, and I will answer directly.

The allegation, as stated, misrepresents my conduct. I have never referred to the Fourth of July as "the holidays." That term, in my usage, refers to the period from late November through early January—encompassing Thanksgiving, Christmas, Hanukkah, Kwanzaa, New Year's, and the general winter observance season.

The Fourth of July I have consistently called "the Fourth of July," "Independence Day," or, on informal occasions, "the Fourth."

*shuffles papers*

However, Mr. Chairman, I will not pretend before this committee that I am without sin. I have, on hot afternoons, referred to it as "the grillin' holidays" in private conversation. I have grouped it with Memorial Day and Labor Day as "the summer long weekends." I may have, in a moment of weakness, typed "July 4th" with the numeral.

But "the holidays"? No, sir. That would be a category error of the highest order. The Fourth stands alone. It requires its own charcoal, its own reverence, its own specific playlist dominated by Springsteen and Sousa in uneasy alliance.

I am prepared to name names, Mr. Chairman. I know who brought the mayonnaise-based potato salad to the 2019 celebration. I know who prematurely detonated the finale cake. 

But I will not confess to a linguistic crime I did not commit.

*leans back*

That is all, Mr. Chairman. God bless America, specifically and exclusively.
